newsitem.title: FRANCE: Forty more die in Algeria's conflict - newspapers.
newsitem.headline: Forty more die in Algeria's conflict - newspapers.

text.p: At least 40 people, mostly civilians including children and a pregnant woman, were killed in Algeria in a new series of attacks over the past three days, Algerian newspapers said on Thursday.
Most of the killings took place in the area known as the "triangle of death", between Algiers, Larba, 25 km (15 miles) to the southeast, and Blida 50 km (30 miles), south of the capital.
Among the dead were at least eight "terrorists" -- Algeria's official term for Moslem fundamentalist rebels -- killed by security forces in Blida province, the papers said.
There was no official confirmation of any of the deaths. The authorities blame the rebels for the violence which has shaken Algeria for nearly six years.

El Watan newspaper said security forces since Monday night had trapped around 100 "terrorists" in Hamam Melouane-Larba region in Blida province. It gave no details on the military operation which follows one in July when newspapers said 300 rebels were killed.
El Watan said in one attack overnight Tuesday-Wednesday, nine people, including three women and three children, were killed in Oued Slama village, Blida province.
Tribune newspaper put the death toll there at seven.
According to El Watan the attackers mined paths to the houses, leaving just one clear for them to use later.

"Caught by surprise by the arrival of security forces, the killers were forced to use one passage they had sown with bombs. Several explosions were heard by residents who said all the elements of the group had been killed," the newspaper said.

Liberte and the influential Arab-language paper Al Khabar reported nine people killed between Larba and Sidi Moussa the same night. Al Khabar said they were all from one family and that security forces had killed some of the group.
Liberte said that on Monday night 11 people were assassinated in Medkhoussa, near Tiaret, some 225 km (140 miles) southwest of Algiers. Six were from one family. All had their throats cut.
Al Khabar also reported 11 killed in Tiaret area. It said among those whose throats were cut were two women, one of whom was nine months pregnant. A tiny child survived the raid.

In an attack in Dahmouni some 20 km (12 miles) from Tiaret, four young men playing dominos outside were killed on Monday, two newspapers said. Liberte said the attackers chained the four together before killing them.

The latest killings follow the slaughter of up to 110 civilians reported by Algerian newspapers on Tuesday, and bring to well over 1,000 people -- including around 300 Moslem rebels -- the number killed since June 5 when Algeria held a general election.
Last Sunday, President Liamine Zeroual vowed to hunt down the killers and called on Algerians to show increased vigilance.

"Abject and barbarous crime, like that which happens on the eve of each determining event in the nation's future, has again shown itself in acts which defy human understanding and challenge the sacred character of human life," he said.

Algeria is preparing for local elections to be held on October 23. Many town halls are run by government appointees after elected officials from the now-outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) were expelled.
El Watan said on Thursday that one of the "terrorists" trapped in Blida province was Mustapha Kartali, "emir" of Larba and a one-time mayor of Larba, elected in 1990 as a FIS candidate.
After being ousted he joined the Armed Islamic Group (GIA), which he quit in a conflict with the then leader Djamel Zitouni.
About 60,000 people have been killed since violence erupted after the authorities in January 1992 cancelled a general election dominated by the FIS.
